<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Sohaib Errabii
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Olivier Sentieys
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Marcello Traiola
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Univ Rennes, Inria, CNRS, IRISA, Rennes, France
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) have garnered significant interest due to their potential for superior parameter efficiency and interpretability compared to Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs). Their key innovation is the use of learnable non-linear activation functions, rather than traditional learnable linear weights.
Those functions are typically parametrized as spline functions, often expressed as linear combinations of basis splines (B-splines). The B-spline coefficients are the model’s new learnable parameters.
However, spline function evaluation significantly increases inference computational complexity.
One conventional way to reduce such complexity is quantization, which reduces the numerical precision of parameters and activations. The impact of quantization on KANs, and especially its effectiveness in reducing computational complexity, is largely unexplored, particularly for quantization levels below 8 bits.
In this work, we examine KANs’ behavior when using existing standard post-training weight and activation quantization and its impact on computational complexity and hardware efficiency.
We find that B-splines are highly robust to quantization and yield substantial reductions in computational complexity, whereas the learnable parameters are more sensitive to quantization.
Hence, we investigate the potential of using low-bit quantized precomputed tables as a replacement for the recursive B-spline algorithm. This approach aims to further reduce the computational complexity of KANs and enhance hardware efficiency while maintaining accuracy.
We performed experiments on six state-of-the-art KAN models, including both MLP-based and convolution-based models. Our results show that B-spline inputs/outputs can be quantized to 2-3 bits with negligible drop in accuracy, while substantially reducing computational complexity.
For example, for ResKAN18, we show that a BitOps reduction of more than <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="50\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\times</annotation></semantics></math> is possible without loss of accuracy, thanks to low-bit quantized B-spline tabulation.
Furthermore, using pre-computed 8-bit lookup tables enables up to <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.9\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.9</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.9\times</annotation></semantics></math> inference speedup on GPUs, while on a systolic-array-based KAN accelerator, reducing the B-spline table precision from 8 to 3 bits on FPGA yields up to 36% resource reduction, 50% higher clock frequency and <math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.24\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.24</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.24\times</annotation></semantics></math> inference speedup. On a 28nm FD-SOI ASIC, reducing the B-spline bit-width from 16 to 3 bits achieves 72% area reduction and 50% higher maximum frequency.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Index Terms: </h6>Quantization, Hardware Acceleration, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, Neural Networks

</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">I </span><span id="S1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Introduction</span></h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) are a new Deep Neural Network (DNN) architecture originally designed as an alternative to Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>.
KANs have gained significant attention and are now used in a range of applications, including time series analysis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>, recommender systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, and medical image segmentation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>. Their main advantages over traditional Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are improved parameter efficiency and explainability.
The primary characteristic that makes KANs unique is the replacement of conventional edge weights with learnable activation functions. For example, learnable <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">spline</span> functions have been used in the original paper <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>.
These splines <math id="S1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> can be expressed as a linear combination of basis functions (<span id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">B-splines</span>) <math id="S1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b()" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b()</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., <math id="S1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi(x)=\sum_{i}w_{i}b_{i}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi(x)=\sum_{i}w_{i}b_{i}(x)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Therefore, in KANs, the learnable parameters are the B-spline coefficients <math id="S1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, from a computational perspective, adding spline function evaluation to the conventional multiplication significantly increases the computational cost, proportionally to the size of the basis. Indeed, to compute KAN inference, instead of performing a single scalar multiplication, each basis function must first be evaluated at the input, followed by a linear combination of all basis functions.
Moreover, their computation is costly because of the B-spline functions’ recursive evaluation (see Section <a href="#S2.SS1" title="II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II-A</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Therefore, research efforts have been focusing on new approaches to accelerate KANs.
Among recent studies, compute-in-memory (CIM) approaches have been proposed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>. In such studies, different ways to approximate the learned non-linear KAN functions or their basis are utilized, such as piece-wise linear (PWL)
approximation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>.
A recent approach <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> focuses on the B-spline evaluation bottleneck. It proposes an efficient dataflow acceleration methods for the Cox-de Boor recursive formula, achieving a significant speedup over CPU and GPU implementations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Another conventional approach to tackling the high computing demands of DNNs is <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">quantization</span>. The quantization process aims at reducing the bit precision of DNN weights and/or activations to low-bit representations (e.g., 8 bits or lower, instead of 32 bits) and to use simpler data types, e.g., fixed-point instead of floating-point. Not only does this reduce the DNN memory requirements, but it also enables the use of simpler and more efficient hardware (e.g., integer arithmetic units instead of floating-point ones) or packing more operands per instruction. In turn, this improves the latency and the overall efficiency.
A recent study had proposed a co-design strategy for efficiently implementing KANs on RRAM-based analog compute-in-memory (CiM) architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>. In this context, a hardware-aware 8-bit quantization method was proposed to reduce the cost of B-spline evaluation, enabling an efficient 8-bit tabulation of B-splines.
More recently, a novel systolic-array-based accelerator that enables efficient end-to-end inference of KANs via non-recursive tabulated 8-bit B-spline evaluation was proposed, achieving a <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup over conventional systolic arrays <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>.
However, the quantization can be pushed to lower precision. A recent preprint studies KAN quantization, evaluating their accuracy loss when low-bit precision is used <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>.
Unfortunately, such work neither studies computational complexity nor proposes methods to leverage quantization to achieve practical computational efficiency (e.g., faster inference, increased clock frequency, or optimized resource utilization). Moreover, it considers only the quantization of KAN’s activations and coefficients, neglecting the quantization of <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">B-spline</span> outputs, and does not explore the quantization space to assess the impact of quantizing the individual KAN tensor components and all their combinations.
A recent paper explores the quantized tabulation of the entire set of KAN learnable <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">spline</span> activation functions and their efficient mapping to FPGA LUT fabrics to reduce computational complexity, avoiding the B-spline basis computation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>. The work highlights encouraging results with low precision (i.e., 5–8 bits).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we explore the impact of standard post-training uniform integer quantization on KANs. Beyond conventional weight and activation quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>, we also consider quantizing B-spline outputs, which are specific to KAN inference and have not been explored previously. We study the impact of quantizing these three components (weights, activations, and B-spline outputs) both in isolation and jointly. Moreover, we study, for the first time, the beneficial effect of KAN’s low-bit quantization on computational complexity by experimenting on GPU and a systolic-array-based KAN hardware accelerator <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>.
We show that the different KANs components exhibit distinct sensitivities to quantization. As also previously highlighted <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>, we find that learnable parameters are particularly sensitive, with significant accuracy degradation below 5 bits for most models. Activations are more resilient than coefficients, tolerating 5-bit quantization with limited impact on accuracy. For the first time, we observe that B-spline outputs are the most resilient, tolerating quantization down to 3 bits for most models. Building on these findings, we explore the use of low-bit quantized precomputed tables to replace the recursive B-spline algorithm, significantly reducing KAN computational complexity while maintaining accuracy. While this has been explored for 8-bit quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, to the best of our knowledge, no evaluation of the computational advantages of low-bit quantized precomputed tables in KAN has been performed.
Our results show that, on a KAN-SAs-style systolic-array accelerator <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> deployed on FPGA, reducing the B-spline table precision from 8 to 3 bits lowers LUT utilization by 36% at the same array size, enables a 50% higher clock frequency, and yields a measured <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.43\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.43</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.43\times</annotation></semantics></math> overall speedup while maintaining accuracy. ASIC synthesis in 28nm FD-SOI shows similar trends. Halving both B-spline and weight precision from 16 to 8 bits reduces cell area by 60% and raises the maximum frequency by 33%, while further reducing B-spline precision to 3 bits achieves an overall 72% area reduction and 50% higher frequency over the 16-bit baseline. Finally, on GPU, using 8-bit B-spline tabulation yields a <math id="S1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.1</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S1.p5.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.9\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.9</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.9\times</annotation></semantics></math> inference speedup with no loss in accuracy.
Finally, we consider the use of low-bit quantized precomputed tables to replace the entire spline computation, as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, and highlight the advantages and limitations of this approach compared to using precomputed tables to replace the recursive B-spline. Our exploration shows that, due to the nature of the two approaches, replacing spline computation is particularly convenient for models of limited dimension, whereas scalability becomes challenging for larger models.
In summary, the contributions of this paper are:</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A comprehensive evaluation of how a standard quantization scheme affects MLP-based and convolutional KANs. The sensitivity of the different tensor components of the KAN layers to quantization is investigated.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An exploration of how combining different quantization levels across KAN tensor components yields different trade-offs between accuracy and computational complexity.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An analysis of the improvements in inference runtime provided by <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">B-spline</span> low-bit quantization and tabulation on GPU and a systolic-array-based KAN hardware accelerator, and the obtained hardware efficiency improvement when synthesizing the latter to FPGA and ASIC.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An analysis of the trade-offs between accuracy and computational complexity achieved through low-bit quantization and tabulation of <span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">splines</span>, as well as its limitations when larger models are utilized.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">II </span><span id="S2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Background and Motivation</span></h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we summarize the theoretical background of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (Section <a href="#S2.SS1" title="II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II-A</span></a>), which essentially involves replacing the weights of conventional neural networks with learnable splines.
In Section <a href="#S2.SS2" title="II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II-B</span></a>, we show the implications of this in terms of computational complexity and number of parameters.
Finally, in Sections <a href="#S2.SS3" title="II-C Uniform Integer Quantization ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II-C</span></a> and <a href="#S2.SS4" title="II-D Activation Function Optimization ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II-D</span></a>, we provide background on the methods used in this work, i.e., uniform integer quantization and tabulation of activation functions, respectively.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">II-A</span> </span><span id="S2.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem</span> states that if <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is a multivariate continuous function on a bounded domain, then <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> can be written as a finite composition of continuous functions of a single variable and the binary operation of addition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>. More specifically,</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(a)=f\left(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\right)=\sum_{q=0}^{2n}\Phi_{q}\left(\sum_{p=1}^{n}\phi_{q,p}\left(a_{p}\right)\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></munderover><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><munderover><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(a)=f\left(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\right)=\sum_{q=0}^{2n}\Phi_{q}\left(\sum_{p=1}^{n}\phi_{q,p}\left(a_{p}\right)\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{q,p}:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbf{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>𝐑</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{q,p}:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbf{R}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi_{q}:\mathbf{R}\rightarrow\mathbf{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>𝐑</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>𝐑</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi_{q}:\mathbf{R}\rightarrow\mathbf{R}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, as there is no smoothness guarantee for these 1D functions, which is known to be critical for deep neural networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>, the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem has not had much success in machine learning.
Recently, a generalization of this theorem defined a single layer that can be stacked to construct neural networks of arbitrary width and depth <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>.
Under this generalization, the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem becomes a particular case of a 2-layer KAN <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[n,2n+1,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[n,2n+1,1]</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., the first layer has <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{in}=n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{in}=n</annotation></semantics></math> input neurons and <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{out}=2n+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{out}=2n+1</annotation></semantics></math> output neurons, and the second one <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{in}=2n+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{in}=2n+1</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{out}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{out}=1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This generic KAN layer can be intuitively pictured as a 2-layer MLP (Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(a)), where the weights at the edges are replaced with learnable activation functions, and the fixed activation (e.g., ReLU) at the nodes is simply replaced with a summation, as depicted in Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(b).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2603.17230v1/kanbspview.png" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:238/119;" width="238" height="119" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 1</span>: </span><span id="S2.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">A single layer of dimensions [2, 2] for MLP (a) and KAN (b). Details of spline computation as a linear combination of B-splines</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To address the missing guarantee of smoothness, the authors proposed to use parameterized splines as the learnable activations <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{q,p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{q,p}</annotation></semantics></math>. Splines are often used to interpolate or approximate data points in a smooth and continuous manner.
To parameterize these splines, various basis functions can be considered, such as Radial Basis Functions (RBF), Fourier, or B-splines <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>. In this work, we focus on the B-spline basis functions (Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(c)) originally proposed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, and widely used in KAN literature. Briefly, B-splines are evaluated as a function of the input (i.e., <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{i,P}(a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{i,P}(a)</annotation></semantics></math>), the results are multiplied by learned coefficients <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and then summed to obtain the spline value <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi(a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi(a)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In more detail, B-spline is a family of piecewise polynomial functions <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{i,P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{i,P}</annotation></semantics></math> defined by its degree <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g., <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P=3</annotation></semantics></math> for cubic
splines as shown in Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Fig. 2 ‣ II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) and a knot vector <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, which specifies the points where the polynomial segments connect.
These functions can be computed by means of the Cox–de Boor recursion formula <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite> as</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{i,P}(a)=\frac{a-t_{i}}{t_{i+P}-t_{i}}b_{i,P-1}(a)+\frac{t_{i+P+1}-a}{t_{i+P+1}-t_{i+1}}b_{i+1,P-1}(a)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{i,P}(a)=\frac{a-t_{i}}{t_{i+P}-t_{i}}b_{i,P-1}(a)+\frac{t_{i+P+1}-a}{t_{i+P+1}-t_{i+1}}b_{i+1,P-1}(a)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.2" class="ltx_p">with</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{i,0}(a)=\begin{cases}1&amp;\text{ if }t_{i}\leq a&lt;t_{i+1}\\
0&amp;\text{ otherwise. }\end{cases}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mtext> if </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mtext> otherwise. </mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{i,0}(a)=\begin{cases}1&amp;\text{ if }t_{i}\leq a&lt;t_{i+1}\\
0&amp;\text{ otherwise. }\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.3" class="ltx_p">The suitability of B-splines as a basis for spline functions is due to a fundamental theorem from Curry and Schoenberg <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>, which states that any spline <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> of degree <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> can be expressed as a linear combination of B-splines, i.e., they form a basis for the spline space:</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{i,j}(a)=\sum_{k}b_{k,P}(a)w_{i,k,j}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>k</mi></munder><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{i,j}(a)=\sum_{k}b_{k,P}(a)w_{i,k,j}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">B-spline basis functions have local support. Indeed, from the Cox-de Boor formula, we can derive that
the function <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{i,P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{i,P}</annotation></semantics></math> is only non-zero in the interval <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[t_{i},t_{i+P+1}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[t_{i},t_{i+P+1}]</annotation></semantics></math>.
The grid <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is defined by first discretizing the input domain (the range of values taken by the KAN layer inputs) into <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> intervals.
The grid is then extended by <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> points on both sides in order to account for all non-zero B-splines within the input domain.
The grid has <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G+2P+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G+2P+1</annotation></semantics></math> points, <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left[t_{0},t_{1},t_{2},\dots,t_{G+2P}\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left[t_{0},t_{1},t_{2},\dots,t_{G+2P}\right]</annotation></semantics></math>, within which <span id="S2.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_bold">G + P</span> non-zero B-splines are needed to evaluate the spline function according to Eq. <a href="#S2.E4" title="In II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.
As an example, Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Fig. 2 ‣ II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reports B-Spline basis functions of degree <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P=3</annotation></semantics></math>. The input domain is divided into <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G=3</annotation></semantics></math> intervals, leading to <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G+2P+1=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G+2P+1=10</annotation></semantics></math> grid points, within which <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G+P=6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G+P=6</annotation></semantics></math> B-splines form a basis for the spline function evaluation. Each B-spline <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{k,3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{k,3}</annotation></semantics></math> is non-zero in the interval <math id="S2.SS1.p6.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[t_{k},t_{k+4}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[t_{k},t_{k+4}]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S2.F2.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S2.F2.3.1" class="ltx_text"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2603.17230v1/bsplines.svg" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:191/72;" width="191" height="72"></object></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 2</span>: </span><span id="S2.F2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">B-Spline basis for <math id="S2.F2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G=3</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.F2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P=3</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.F2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G+2P+1=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G+2P+1=10</annotation></semantics></math> grid points <math id="S2.F2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[t_{0},\dots,t_{9}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>9</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[t_{0},\dots,t_{9}]</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, as reported in Eq. <a href="#S2.E4" title="In II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and sketched in Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(b-c), evaluating <math id="S2.SS1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{i,j}(a_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{i,j}(a_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> involves computing the <math id="S2.SS1.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G+P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G+P</annotation></semantics></math> B-splines at <math id="S2.SS1.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, multiplying each by its corresponding learnable coefficient, and summing the results. Then, as indicated in Eq. <a href="#S2.E5" title="In II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, all the spline functions are aggregated to produce the output of the layer.</p>
<table id="S2.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{(l+1)}_{j}=\sum_{i=0}^{N^{(l)}_{in}}\sum_{k=0}^{N_{b}-1}b_{k,P}(a^{(l)}_{i})w^{(l)}_{i,k,j}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></munderover><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{(l+1)}_{j}=\sum_{i=0}^{N^{(l)}_{in}}\sum_{k=0}^{N_{b}-1}b_{k,P}(a^{(l)}_{i})w^{(l)}_{i,k,j}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p7.2" class="ltx_p">This is equivalent to a matrix multiplication of the form,</p>
<table id="S2.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l+1)}=B^{(l)}W^{(l)}=b(A^{(l)})W^{(l)}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l+1)}=B^{(l)}W^{(l)}=b(A^{(l)})W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Convolutional KAN:</span> The KAN operation can also be applied to convolution by replacing the scalar filter weights with learnable activations.
In practice, similarly to how standard convolution can be implemented as im2col followed by matrix multiplication <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, a convolutional KAN unfolds the input feature map into a matrix of patches, then applies the same KAN operation.
An open-source implementation of this ConvKAN operation is available in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>. Efficient training and design of CNN networks based on this convolution operation have also been studied in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>.
In this paper, to distinguish between the MLP- and CNN-based KANs, we refer to the convolutional one as <span id="S2.SS1.p8.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ConvKAN</span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">II-B</span> </span><span id="S2.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Increased number of operations in KANs</span></h3>

<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S2.F3.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S2.F3.3.1" class="ltx_text"><img src="2603.17230v1/kanbspview_new.png" id="S2.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/363;" width="476" height="363" alt="Refer to caption"></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 3</span>: </span><span id="S2.F3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The compute graph of a KAN layer <math id="S2.F3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> consists of B-spline evaluation followed by a standard matrix multiplication. </span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> sketches a KAN layer <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">l</span> from a computational perspective. Firstly, B-splines are evaluated as a function of an activation matrix <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, which generates an intermediate matrix <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{l}</annotation></semantics></math>. The latter is then multiplied by the matrix of learned coefficients <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{l}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The dimensions of the matrices <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> are respectively <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\times N_{in}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\times N_{in}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\times N_{in}^{l}(G+P)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\times N_{in}^{l}(G+P)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{in}^{l}(G+P)\times N_{out}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{in}^{l}(G+P)\times N_{out}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> is the batch size and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{in}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{in}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{out}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{out}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> the number of input and output neurons of the layer <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">l</span>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S2.SS2.SSS1.6" class="ltx_text">II-B</span>1 </span>Increased model parameters and number of operations</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although KANs are more parameter efficient than the non-KAN counterpart <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, parameterization using a function basis leads to an increase in model parameters by a factor of <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G+P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G+P</annotation></semantics></math>, compared to non-KAN MLPs or CNNs, for the same layer dimension <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left[N^{l}_{in},N^{l}_{out}\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>[</mo><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left[N^{l}_{in},N^{l}_{out}\right]</annotation></semantics></math>.
For instance, a KAN layer with cubic B-splines (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P=3</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G=5</annotation></semantics></math>) would have <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="8\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8\times</annotation></semantics></math> as many parameters as an MLP layer of the same dimensions.
This, in turn, increases the computational effort required. Indeed, the number of multiply-accumulate operations to perform the <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}\times W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}\times W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> matrix multiplication of Eq. <a href="#S2.E6" title="In II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> is <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N^{(l)}_{in}\cdot(G+P)\cdot M\cdot N^{(l)}_{out}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N^{(l)}_{in}\cdot(G+P)\cdot M\cdot N^{(l)}_{out}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S2.F4.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S2.F4.3.1" class="ltx_text"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2603.17230v1/coxtriangle.svg" id="S2.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:191/127;" width="191" height="127"></object></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 4</span>: </span><span id="S2.F4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Cox-de Boor evaluation triangle for B-splines <math id="S2.F4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{3,3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{3,3}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.F4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{4,3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{4,3}</annotation></semantics></math> of degree <math id="S2.F4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P=3</annotation></semantics></math>.
Each row corresponds to the recursive computations of <math id="S2.F4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{i,P}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{i,P}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> from <math id="S2.F4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{i,P-1}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{i,P-1}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.F4.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{i+1,P-1}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{i+1,P-1}(x)</annotation></semantics></math>.
The number of required B-splines in every row decreases linearly with <math id="S2.F4.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>, leading to the total number of operations in Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="TABLE I ‣ II-B1 Increased model parameters and number of operations ‣ II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the B-spline evaluation (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}=b(A^{(l)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}=b(A^{(l)})</annotation></semantics></math>), most KAN implementations rely on an iterative and parallel version of the Cox-de Boor formula of Eq. <a href="#S2.E2" title="In II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> to compute <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{b}=G+P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{b}=G+P</annotation></semantics></math> B-splines of degree <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>. Figure <a href="#S2.F4" title="Fig. 4 ‣ II-B1 Increased model parameters and number of operations ‣ II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> conceptually illustrates it for only two B-splines, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{3,3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{3,3}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{4,3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{4,3}</annotation></semantics></math>, of Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Fig. 2 ‣ II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
As shown in the first row of the figure, the algorithm starts by evaluating the five B-splines of degree <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> (cf. Eq. <a href="#S2.E3" title="In II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) contributing to <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{3,3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{3,3}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{4,3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{4,3}</annotation></semantics></math>, then iteratively at each row <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> it evaluates the B-splines of degree <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> according to Eq. <a href="#S2.E3" title="In II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> until the row <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d=P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=P</annotation></semantics></math>. In the general form, it starts with <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G+2P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G+2P</annotation></semantics></math> B-splines of degree <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=0</annotation></semantics></math>. Then, iteratively at each row <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>, it evaluates the <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G+2P-d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G+2P-d</annotation></semantics></math> B-splines of degree
<math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> until the row <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d=P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=P</annotation></semantics></math>.
Under the hypothesis that the reciprocals of the grid differences (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{i+P}-t_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{i+P}-t_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{i+P+1}-t_{i+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{i+P+1}-t_{i+1}</annotation></semantics></math>) are precomputed, four multiplications are needed per B-spline evaluation.
This is performed for the whole layer input matrix <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> of size <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\times N^{(l)}_{in}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\times N^{(l)}_{in}</annotation></semantics></math> leading to <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4MN^{(l)}_{in}(P(G+2P)-\frac{P(P-1)}{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4MN^{(l)}_{in}(P(G+2P)-\frac{P(P-1)}{2})</annotation></semantics></math> multiplications.
We report in Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="TABLE I ‣ II-B1 Increased model parameters and number of operations ‣ II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a> the number of arithmetic multiplications (MULs) for an MLP layer versus a KAN layer.
When it comes to convolutional KANs, most implementations rely on lowering the convolution operation to a matrix multiplication using the im2col technique <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>.
Therefore, to obtain the arithmetic complexity of ConvKAN, we can replace <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{out}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{out}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{in}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{in}</annotation></semantics></math> in Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="TABLE I ‣ II-B1 Increased model parameters and number of operations ‣ II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a> respectively by <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{out}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{out}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K^{2}C_{in}H_{out}W_{out}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K^{2}C_{in}H_{out}W_{out}</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> the filter size, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{out},W_{out}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{out},W_{out}</annotation></semantics></math> the output image size, and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{in},C_{out}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{in},C_{out}</annotation></semantics></math> the input and output number of channels.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">From these considerations, we can estimate the computational complexity of KANs and explore the impact of quantization.
To do so, we estimate the number of operations using the conventional <span id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BitOps</span> metric <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>. With such a metric, the cost of multiplying <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>-bit and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>-bit integers can be approximated to <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\times m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\times m</annotation></semantics></math> binary operations.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table">
