<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We define the bit-widths of the activations <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, the intermediate tensor of B-spline evaluations <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the weights <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> as <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{A^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{A^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{B^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{B^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{W^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{W^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively.
Then, based on the number of multiplications reported in Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="TABLE I ‣ II-B1 Increased model parameters and number of operations ‣ II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>, the multiplication BitOps for the a KAN layer <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> can be approximated as</p>
<table id="S2.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">The last term in Eq. <a href="#S2.E7" title="In II-B1 Increased model parameters and number of operations ‣ II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw^{2}_{A^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw^{2}_{A^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math>, results from the Cox-de Boor recursion, where each multiplication has both operands involving activations (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>), hence having the same bitwidth <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{A^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{A^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> (see Eq. <a href="#S2.E3" title="In II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), unlike the matrix multiply involving B-spline and weights, hence having bit-width <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{B^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{B^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{W^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{W^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In comparison, the BitOps resulting from multiplications in the MLP layer does not include the additional term due to B-spline evaluation:</p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{BitOps}^{(l)}_{MLP}=MN_{out}^{l}N_{in}^{l}bw_{A^{(l)}}bw_{W^{(l)}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mtext>BitOps</mtext><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{BitOps}^{(l)}_{MLP}=MN_{out}^{l}N_{in}^{l}bw_{A^{(l)}}bw_{W^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Eq. <a href="#S2.E7" title="In II-B1 Increased model parameters and number of operations ‣ II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> shows that the bit-width of the activations, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{A^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{A^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math>, only impacts the arithmetic cost of the B-spline evaluation, while the bit-width of the weights <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> and intermediate tensor <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> (i.e., <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{W^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{W^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{B^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{B^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> respectively) contribute to the arithmetic cost of matrix multiplication.
In this paper, we study how quantizing weights, B-splines, and activations reduces BitOps and mitigates the intrinsic increase in model parameters and operations in KANs. In Section <a href="#S3" title="III KANtize Approach ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III</span></a>, we further elaborate on how quantization reduces KAN computational complexity, and, building on this, how the tabulation of B-splines and learned splines further reduces it.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.6" class="ltx_text">II-B</span>2 </span>Computational overhead of B-spline evaluation</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to the increased number of operations, the evaluation of the <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G+P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G+P</annotation></semantics></math> B-splines with the recursive Cox-de Boor formula is not accelerated efficiently on GPUs due to the interdependencies introduced by the recursion, which intrinsically serializes the computation.
This directly impacts the inference latency.
In particular, as further shown in Section <a href="#S4" title="IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV</span></a>, the B-spline evaluation completely dominates the latency of the forward pass. For instance, as reported in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="TABLE III ‣ IV-B3 Latency Improvement ‣ IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III</span></a>, the B-spline computation accounts for up to <span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_bold">98%</span> of the total inference time for MLP-based KANs, and <span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_bold">78</span>–<span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_bold">84%</span> for convolutional models where the im2col overhead reduces the B-spline contribution.
Therefore, for KANs, it is important to accelerate the evaluation of the basis functions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>.
Similarly to what is shown in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> for a CiM-based and systolic-array-based accelerators, respectively, we show in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="III-B B-spline Tabulation ‣ III KANtize Approach ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III-B</span></a> that this issue can be addressed in GPUs by replacing the recursive computations of B-splines with precomputed lookup tables (LUTs). This significantly reduces inference latency with negligible memory overhead and accuracy drop, as shown in the results reported in Section <a href="#S4" title="IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV</span></a>. Moreover, we show that dedicated hardware <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> enables further improvements in KAN efficiency thanks to low-bit quantization.
Finally, in Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="III-C Spline Tabulation and Quantization ‣ III KANtize Approach ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III-C</span></a> we study the opportunities and challenges of a multiplier-free approach that uses low-bit-quantized precomputed tables to replace the entire <span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">spline</span> computation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">II-C</span> </span><span id="S2.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Uniform Integer Quantization</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Quantization has been extensively studied as an approach to reduce the memory footprint and inference latency of DNNs.
In this work, we focus on uniform integer quantization, which consists of mapping a floating-point range <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\alpha,\beta]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\alpha,\beta]</annotation></semantics></math> to an integer range <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\alpha_{q},\beta_{q}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\alpha_{q},\beta_{q}]</annotation></semantics></math> that is representable by the considered precision (bit-width).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The linear transformation to map a real number <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> to an integer <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{q}</annotation></semantics></math> is parameterized with
<math id="S2.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s\in\mathbf{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>𝐑</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s\in\mathbf{R}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z\in\mathbf{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>𝐙</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\in\mathbf{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> as follows:</p>

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\operatorname{dequantize}(x_{q},s,z)=s(x_{q}-z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>dequantize</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\operatorname{dequantize}(x_{q},s,z)=s(x_{q}-z)</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{clip}(x;a,b):=\min(\max(x,a),b)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>clip</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{clip}(x;a,b):=\min(\max(x,a),b)</annotation></semantics></math>.
The parameters <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s,z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s,z</annotation></semantics></math> are computed by mapping the floating-point bounds <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\alpha,\beta]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\alpha,\beta]</annotation></semantics></math> to the quantization range bounds <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[\alpha_{q},\beta_{q}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\alpha_{q},\beta_{q}]</annotation></semantics></math> as follows:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E11"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E12.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\operatorname{round}\left(\frac{\beta\alpha_{q}-\alpha\beta_{q}}{\beta-\alpha}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>round</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\operatorname{round}\left(\frac{\beta\alpha_{q}-\alpha\beta_{q}}{\beta-\alpha}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS4.6" class="ltx_text">II-D</span> </span><span id="S2.SS4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Activation Function Optimization</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In digital neural networks, non-linear activations can be categorized into two main approaches from a computational perspective: (i) direct algorithmic implementation of the functions and (ii) use of precomputed Look-Up Tables (LUT) to replace the computation.
The first approach is generally implemented either by composing elementary functions (e.g., exponential, reciprocal, etc.) or by approximating them mathematically, for instance, with a polynomial.
This approach has been studied in various works, especially for architectures such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) that require multiple evaluations of non-linear activation functions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>. However, these works primarily focus on specific functions common in neural networks, such as the <math id="S2.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="tanh" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">tanh</annotation></semantics></math> activation function <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>.
In the second approach, precomputed activation function samples are stored in the LUT. The LUT is then accessed using the result of the previous layer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>, and the corresponding precomputed output value is used.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As KANs rely even more heavily on activation functions than RNNs, these techniques become much more critical. Indeed, a feed-forward KAN layer consists of <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{in}\cdot N_{out}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{in}\cdot N_{out}</annotation></semantics></math> spline functions, while ConvKAN has <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K^{2}\cdot C_{in}\cdot C_{out}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K^{2}\cdot C_{in}\cdot C_{out}</annotation></semantics></math> functions. In turn, as already mentioned, each spline is composed of <math id="S2.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(G+P)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(G+P)</annotation></semantics></math> B-splines.
In the context of the KAN activation functions, combining low-bit integer quantization and precomputed look-up tables has a twofold effect: (i) reducing the latency of computing the non-linear activation functions by reducing the amount of data to process and the computation complexity, and (ii) reducing the memory cost when using precomputed look-up tables for activation functions. The remainder of the paper presents the proposed approach for combining these two methods, aiming to achieve latency and memory improvements without compromising accuracy.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">III </span><span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">KANtize Approach</span></h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we explore the quantization and tabulation opportunities in KANs and combine them.
Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="III-A Exploring the Quantization of KANs’ Weights, Activations and B-splines ‣ III KANtize Approach ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III-A</span></a> elaborates how quantization helps address the issue of increased model parameters and BitOps complexity. In particular, we discuss how quantizing the different KAN tensor components (<math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>) affects computational complexity.
Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="III-B B-spline Tabulation ‣ III KANtize Approach ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III-B</span></a> illustrates how to efficiently implement the B-spline <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b()" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b()</annotation></semantics></math> quantized tabulation scheme that helps address the inference bottleneck of the recursive <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">B-spline</span> evaluation.
Finally, Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="III-C Spline Tabulation and Quantization ‣ III KANtize Approach ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III-C</span></a> illustrates the tabulation of the learned <span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">splines</span> <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi()" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi()</annotation></semantics></math> (see Eq. <a href="#S2.E4" title="In II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>), which completely replaces the B-spline evaluation and their linear combination depicted in Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(c), and allows computing a KAN layer by visiting the tables and summing their values.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S3.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">III-A</span> </span><span id="S3.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Exploring the Quantization of KANs’ Weights, Activations and B-splines</span></h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, from a computational perspective, weight quantization in a KAN layer is similar to MLP layers, with the coefficients of the basis functions acting as the weights (i.e., <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>).
Hence, when we apply conventional uniform integer weight quantization techniques to the KAN’s coefficients, i.e., we reduce <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{W^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{W^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> in Eq. <a href="#S2.E7" title="In II-B1 Increased model parameters and number of operations ‣ II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, this significantly reduces the memory cost of weights and the BitOps complexity of the matrix multiply.
In MLPs, quantizing both weights <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> and activations <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., reducing <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{W^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{W^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{A^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{A^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> in Eq. <a href="#S2.E8" title="In II-B1 Increased model parameters and number of operations ‣ II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, not only further reduces the memory cost and BitOps of the matrix multiplication but also enables more efficient hardware utilization, allowing the use of integer arithmetic pipelines or integer tensor cores. In KANs, since the B-spline outputs are used in the matrix multiplication, to achieve similar benefits we quantize the intermediate B-spline evaluation tensor, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., we reduce <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{B^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{B^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> in Eq. <a href="#S2.E7" title="In II-B1 Increased model parameters and number of operations ‣ II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. Finally, quantization of activations <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> in KANs is helpful for reducing the memory and BitOps cost of computing the B-splines, i.e., reducing <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{A^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{A^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> in Eq. <a href="#S2.E7" title="In II-B1 Increased model parameters and number of operations ‣ II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.
As shown in Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="TABLE I ‣ II-B1 Increased model parameters and number of operations ‣ II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>, if <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{out}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{out}</annotation></semantics></math> is not too large, then the BitOps cost of B-spline evaluation can be as significant as the matrix multiplication.
Therefore, to properly address the computational issues of KAN, it is important to consider quantizing all three <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> and investigating their combination.
The results of this exploration are reported in Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="IV-A Quantization Space Exploration: Accuracy vs BitOps ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S3.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">III-B</span> </span><span id="S3.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">B-spline Tabulation</span></h3>

<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2603.17230v1/bsplinelutstrat.svg" id="S3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/174;" width="429" height="174"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 5</span>: </span><span id="S3.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Only half the values of one B-spline need to be stored (e.g., half of <math id="S3.F5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{3,3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{3,3}</annotation></semantics></math>, colored in black), and the other B-splines can be evaluated by translating the input and using symmetry.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2603.17230v1/bspline_tabulation.svg" id="S3.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/252;" width="405" height="252"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 6</span>: </span><span id="S3.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Tabulation of the canonical B-spline <math id="S3.F6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{0,3}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{0,3}(x)</annotation></semantics></math>: only the first half is stored with <math id="S3.F6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{k}</annotation></semantics></math> entries per knot interval <math id="S3.F6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[t_{i},t_{i+1}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[t_{i},t_{i+1}]</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2603.17230v1/bspline_naive_tabulation.svg" id="S3.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/259;" width="405" height="259"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 7</span>: </span><span id="S3.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Naive tabulation example with <math id="S3.F7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G=15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G=15</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.F7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=4</annotation></semantics></math>: uniform quantization to <math id="S3.F7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{k}</annotation></semantics></math> levels wastes entries in zero regions, capturing only 5 of 16 entries for the B-spline.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As discussed in Section <a href="#S2.SS2" title="II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II-B</span></a>, the inefficiency of the recursive B-splines evaluation can be addressed by replacing the recursive computations with precomputed LUTs, significantly reducing inference latency.
As pointed out in previous literature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> and depicted in the example in Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Fig. 5 ‣ III-B B-spline Tabulation ‣ III KANtize Approach ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> (adapted from Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Fig. 2 ‣ II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), in the case of a uniform grid, we only need to tabulate half of a single canonical B-spline (highlighted in black in the figure). Then, we can infer the remaining elements from simple symmetry and translation.
For example, for a given input <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, only the value <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{3,3}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{3,3}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> would be saved in the LUT, while the value <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{1,3}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{1,3}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> could be obtained by retrieving the value <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{3,3}(t_{5}-(x-t_{3}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{3,3}(t_{5}-(x-t_{3}))</annotation></semantics></math>, which is the same, as shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Fig. 5 ‣ III-B B-spline Tabulation ‣ III KANtize Approach ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.
This enables a <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">single compact LUT</span> to serve all KAN layers, regardless of model depth, grid size, or input range.
When the grid is adapted to each layer’s inputs during training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, the non-uniform knot spacing breaks translation invariance and would require separate tables.
However, techniques such as least-squares fitting enable approximating a general spline using a uniform B-spline basis, achieving arbitrary precision with a sufficiently fine grid.
Without loss of generality, this work focuses on uniform grids. A separate LUT would be needed only for each distinct spline degree <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To build the LUT, the canonical B-spline is evaluated at equidistant points within each knot interval of the stored half-support, with boundary points mapped exactly to zero to avoid accumulated errors outside the
local support.
As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S3.F6" title="Fig. 6 ‣ III-B B-spline Tabulation ‣ III KANtize Approach ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, when the tensor <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> is quantized to <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=bw_{A^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=bw_{A^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> bits, the LUT contains <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{k}</annotation></semantics></math> entries per knot interval <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[t_{i},t_{i+1}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[t_{i},t_{i+1}]</annotation></semantics></math>.
For example, <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\!=\!2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0.108em">=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\!=\!2</annotation></semantics></math> yields a coarse staircase of <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math> entries in each interval, e.g., [1,2], while <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\!=\!4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0.108em">=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\!=\!4</annotation></semantics></math> gives <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>16</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16</annotation></semantics></math> entries and a much tighter approximation.
This contrasts with a naive strategy that uniformly quantizes the full input domain into <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{k}</annotation></semantics></math> levels.
As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F7" title="Fig. 7 ‣ III-B B-spline Tabulation ‣ III KANtize Approach ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, most entries would fall outside the B-spline’s narrow local support, wasting storage and yielding a poor approximation, especially at higher <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The values stored in the LUT can also be quantized to <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=bw_{B^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=bw_{B^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> bits, corresponding to the quantization of tensor <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>. We refer to the resulting configuration as a <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k{\times}h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k{\times}h</annotation></semantics></math> LUT.
This notation denotes the quantization bit-widths, not the table dimensions. Since the half-support spans <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lceil(P+1)/2\rceil" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌈</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌉</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lceil(P+1)/2\rceil</annotation></semantics></math> knot intervals with <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{k}</annotation></semantics></math> entries of <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> bits each, the actual LUT memory is <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{k}\times\lceil(P+1)/2\rceil\times h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌈</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">⌉</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{k}\times\lceil(P+1)/2\rceil\times h</annotation></semantics></math> bits.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">As highlighted in previous research <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, tabulation further reduces the computational complexity, as it replaces the cost of recursively computing the B-spline values with the cost of fetching data from a LUT. Also, it ensures that the LUT only stores the non-zero B-spline values. However, without specialized hardware support for efficient sparsity management (e.g., as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>), reconstructing the complete sparse matrix is necessary to perform matrix multiplication with the coefficients.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We study, for the first time, the effects of tabulating the B-splines with different <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> low-bit values in terms of the trade-off between accuracy and memory needed to store them. Furthermore, we evaluate the gains in terms of BitOps reduction and how they translate to inference latency reduction. The inference latency gains, of course, depend on the HW support. For instance, GPUs only support specific bit-widths natively (e.g., 8 bits), and would not gain in latency when using lower-bit quantizations (e.g., less than 8 bits). However, using custom hardware allows further improvement in latency when using lower-bit quantizations. The results of the study are presented in Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S3.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">III-C</span> </span><span id="S3.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Spline Tabulation and Quantization</span></h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we explore the impact of low-bit quantization on a multiplier-free KAN inference.
Instead of obtaining the learned splines through linear decomposition in the B-spline basis followed by matrix multiplication (as shown in Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), we directly tabulate each learned function independently on the
extended grid domain, as also shown in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>. Thus, given a layer of dimensions <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left[N_{in},N_{out}\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>[</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left[N_{in},N_{out}\right]</annotation></semantics></math>, the only operations remaining after tabulation of the splines are
the <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{in}\cdot N_{out}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{in}\cdot N_{out}</annotation></semantics></math> additions that sum the values retrieved from the corresponding <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{in}\cdot N_{out}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{in}\cdot N_{out}</annotation></semantics></math> spline tables.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2603.17230v1/spline_table_single_layer.svg" id="S3.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:429/373;" width="429" height="373"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 8</span>: </span><span id="S3.F8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Example of a learned spline in the single-layer KAN <math id="S3.F8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[784,10]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>784</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[784,10]</annotation></semantics></math> for different <math id="S3.F8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> values. The legend shows the number of bits used for input quantization.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F8" title="Fig. 8 ‣ III-C Spline Tabulation and Quantization ‣ III KANtize Approach ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> shows examples of different splines tabulated by sampling the inputs with different bit-widths and for different <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> values. For example, when inputs are quantized with <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{A^{(l)}}\!=\!3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{A^{(l)}}\!=\!3</annotation></semantics></math> bits, the resulting table has <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{3}=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{3}=8</annotation></semantics></math> entries, each storing the spline output value at the corresponding quantized input level (red curve).
Similar to B-spline tabulation, the values stored in the spline tables can also be quantized to
For comparison, the original FP32 coefficients require <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(G+P)\cdot 32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(G+P)\cdot 32</annotation></semantics></math> bits per connection.
further reduce memory cost. Indeed, the memory cost is significant in this case because the table dimension scales with the layer dimensions. A single KAN layer leads to <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{in}\cdot N_{out}\cdot 2^{(bw_{A^{(l)}})}\cdot h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{in}\cdot N_{out}\cdot 2^{(bw_{A^{(l)}})}\cdot h</annotation></semantics></math> stored bits when using <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>-bit quantized spline values and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{(bw_{A^{(l)}})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{(bw_{A^{(l)}})}</annotation></semantics></math> table entries.
For configurations where <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{(bw_{A^{(l)}})}\cdot h&lt;(G+P)\cdot 32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{(bw_{A^{(l)}})}\cdot h&lt;(G+P)\cdot 32</annotation></semantics></math>,
the spline table would actually be smaller than the FP32 <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> coefficients it replaces.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The quantization parameters can be computed without requiring any calibration, which is a direct benefit of the local support
property of B-splines. Since all individual B-spline functions are zero outside their respective grid intervals (as
illustrated in Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Fig. 2 ‣ II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), any linear combination of these splines will also be zero outside the overall grid
range. This characteristic enables us to utilize the defined grid range for computing the quantization parameters, thereby
simplifying the process by eliminating the need for calibration data.
For example, as shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F8" title="Fig. 8 ‣ III-C Spline Tabulation and Quantization ‣ III KANtize Approach ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, all splines of a given layer share the same grid and are zero outside the extended grid range. Therefore, the quantization range for the input can be set directly to the grid bounds, since any activation falling outside this range would have zero contribution regardless of its actual value.
Furthermore, the same grid is often used across the KAN layers. Thus, the same quantization parameters are used to map the previous layer’s output to an integer for addressing the spline tables.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scalability of spline tabulation</span>:
While spline tabulation eliminates multiplications, the total number of spline tables scales with <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{l}N_{in}^{(l)}\cdot N_{out}^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>l</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{l}N_{in}^{(l)}\cdot N_{out}^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, which grows quickly with model size. The implications of this scaling for both GPU inference latency and FPGA resource cost are studied in Section <a href="#S4.SS3.SSS2" title="IV-C2 Latency Improvement ‣ IV-C Spline Tabulation space exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-C2</span></a> and Section <a href="#S4.SS3.SSS3" title="IV-C3 Scalability of Spline Tabulation on FPGA ‣ IV-C Spline Tabulation space exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-C3</span></a>, respectively.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">IV </span><span id="S4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Experimental Results</span></h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In line with previous work on KANs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, in our evaluation we focus on the two state-of-the-art KAN families, MLP-based and ConvKAN, that we can feasibly train for classification on MNIST and CIFAR-10, given the lack of open-source pretrained KAN models.
For MNIST classification, we use MLP-based KANs and a ConvKAN model based on LeNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite> with two ConvKAN layers followed by a single feed-forward KAN layer. For <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">CIFAR-10</span>, we study two simple convolutional models, CNN3 and CNN4, with three and four ConvKAN layers, respectively, and a ResNet18-based model in which convolutions are replaced by ConvKAN layers and thus called ResKAN18.
Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="TABLE II ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II</span></a> summarizes the models, datasets, and number of parameters.</p>
</div>

<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For all models, we consider that all KAN layers in a given model have the same <math id="S4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> parameters and a uniform grid that is not updated during training. Unless otherwise specified, all models were trained without using the bias based on SiLU, suggested by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>.
This bias is, in fact, an independent MLP branch, and thus significantly impacts the training and the resulting weight distribution between actual basis function coefficients and the scaling used for SiLU. In this paper, we focus on studying the behavior of the spline-based KAN operation itself.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we report the results of the described quantization and tabulation approaches on the models.
Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="IV-A Quantization Space Exploration: Accuracy vs BitOps ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-A</span></a> reports the results of quantization in terms of the trade-off between accuracy and BitOps reduction.
Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-B</span></a> studies the trade-off between accuracy and memory reduction thanks to B-spline tabulation, and discusses the results concerning the improvements in inference latency obtained through tabulation.
Finally, Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="IV-C Spline Tabulation space exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-C</span></a> examines these same aspects for spline tabulation and the associated scalability challenges.</p>
</div>
