The bit-widths of <math id="S4.F9.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.F9.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.F9.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> are encoded by marker colors, sizes, and shapes, respectively.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As mentioned in Sections <a href="#S2.SS2" title="II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II-B</span></a> and <a href="#S3.SS1" title="III-A Exploring the Quantization of KANs’ Weights, Activations and B-splines ‣ III KANtize Approach ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III-A</span></a>, the quantization of the different tensor components of the KAN layer <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> impacts the computational cost (measured in BitOps using Eq. <a href="#S2.E7" title="In II-B1 Increased model parameters and number of operations ‣ II-B Increased number of operations in KANs ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>) and the model’s accuracy differently.
To isolate the effect of each, we first quantize only one component at a time
while holding the other components at their baseline precision of 32 bits.
Figures <a href="#S4.F9" title="Fig. 9 ‣ IV-A Quantization Space Exploration: Accuracy vs BitOps ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> (a,b,c,g,h,i) report accuracy vs BitOps results for the six models described in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="TABLE II ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II</span></a> when quantizing only one component of the KAN layer at a time, i.e., <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>.
As shown in these figures, the weight matrix <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> is the most sensitive to quantization, consistent with previous findings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>.
Concerning the activation matrix <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, we observe it is less sensitive overall than <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> (with the exception of LeKAN), but contributes less to BitOps reduction, as anticipated in Section <a href="#S3" title="III KANtize Approach ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III</span></a>.
Finally, we characterize, for the first time, the quantization sensitivity of <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, the intermediate tensor of B-spline activations, which proves quite robust.
For instance, the CNN3 model, trained on CIFAR-10, has a sharp accuracy drop of <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 12\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>12</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 12\%</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> quantized to 5 bits, whereas it only drops by <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\%</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> at the same bit-width and practically shows no degradation for <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> quantized to 5 and even 4 bits.
More generally, all models maintain nearly full accuracy even when <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> is quantized to 3 or 4 bits, with CNN3 being the most sensitive (<math id="S4.SS1.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 3.5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>3.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 3.5\%</annotation></semantics></math> drop at 3 bits). Moreover, quantizing <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> also greatly contributes to BitOps reduction.
The CNN and ResKAN models exhibit the largest relative savings. For instance, quantizing <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math>-bits in the ResKAN18 model reduces BitOps from <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 4\times 10^{9}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>9</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 4\times 10^{9}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 6\times 10^{8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>8</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 6\times 10^{8}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., almost one order of magnitude reduction. The CNN4 model shows a similarly strong drop in BitOps from <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4.83\times 10^{9}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4.83</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>9</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4.83\times 10^{9}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="6.5\times 10^{8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>6.5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>8</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6.5\times 10^{8}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Then, we quantize all the tensor components of the KAN layer, <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, at the same time, and explore all combinatorial bit-width reduction possibilities. In Figure <a href="#S4.F9" title="Fig. 9 ‣ IV-A Quantization Space Exploration: Accuracy vs BitOps ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> (d,e,f,j,k,l), we report the obtained Pareto-front in terms of Accuracy vs BitOps trade-off, i.e., the best quantization combinations of <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>. For easier comparison, we align the x-axis values across graphs showing the same model (e.g., a and d).
As expected, across all tested models, the combined quantization yields a consistent reduction in BitOPs compared to quantizing the KAN components one at a time, without loss of accuracy. For example, for ResKAN18, while quantizing the single <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> component allowed reducing the BitOPs by almost an order of magnitude (from <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 4\times 10^{9}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>9</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 4\times 10^{9}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 6\times 10^{8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>8</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 6\times 10^{8}</annotation></semantics></math>) without accuracy loss (Figure <a href="#S4.F9" title="Fig. 9 ‣ IV-A Quantization Space Exploration: Accuracy vs BitOps ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>(i)), the combined quantization allowed further reduction of more than 60% (<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 2\times 10^{8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>8</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 2\times 10^{8}</annotation></semantics></math>) without accuracy loss (Figure <a href="#S4.F9" title="Fig. 9 ‣ IV-A Quantization Space Exploration: Accuracy vs BitOps ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>(l)).
In general, we observe that solutions providing both high accuracy and BitOps reductions typically use <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> quantization with 5-8 bits (i.e., red, purple, and pink colors in the graphs), while <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> quantization values are most of the time as low as 3 bits (i.e., pentagon shape in the graphs), and <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> quantization values typically range from 5 to 8 bits with some models going as low as 4 bits (e.g., KANMLP1 KANMLP2 and LeKAN). <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> quantization values lower than 5 (i.e., green and orange colors) mostly entail substantial accuracy drops, as also happens for <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> quantization values lower than 4 or 5.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">IV-B</span> </span><span id="S4.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this subsection, we explore the space of possible B-Spline tabulation opportunities and show the effects in terms of accuracy vs memory tradeoff (Sec. <a href="#S4.SS2.SSS1" title="IV-B1 Accuracy vs Memory tradeoff ‣ IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-B1</span></a>), accuracy vs computational complexity (Sec. <a href="#S4.SS2.SSS2" title="IV-B2 Accuracy vs Computational Complexity ‣ IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-B2</span></a>), inference latency on GPUs and a systolic-array-based hardware accelerator, i.e., KAN-SAs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> (Sec. <a href="#S4.SS2.SSS3" title="IV-B3 Latency Improvement ‣ IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-B3</span></a>), and area and frequency scaling of the latter (Sec. <a href="#S4.SS2.SSS4" title="IV-B4 KAN-SAs Area and Frequency Scaling ‣ IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-B4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS1.6" class="ltx_text">IV-B</span>1 </span>Accuracy vs Memory tradeoff</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In Figure <a href="#S4.F10" title="Fig. 10 ‣ IV-B1 Accuracy vs Memory tradeoff ‣ IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, we report the Pareto front of accuracy versus LUT memory for each model with fixed 8-bit weights <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>, varying the addressing bit-width <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{A^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{A^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> and stored value bit-width <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{B^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{B^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Some plots do not report solutions with higher bit widths (e.g., KANMPL1) since they were Pareto-dominated by the reported low-bit-width ones.
For all models, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{B^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{B^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> can be reduced to 3 or 4 bits with minimal accuracy loss, with associated LUT memory gains up to more than one order of magnitude when moving from 8 bits (X shape) to 3 (pentagon) or 2 (dot) bits, confirming the robustness of the B-spline activations already observed in Figure <a href="#S4.F9" title="Fig. 9 ‣ IV-A Quantization Space Exploration: Accuracy vs BitOps ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>.
The addressing bit-width <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{A^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{A^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> has the largest impact on LUT memory due to the exponential scaling (<math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{(bw_{A^{(l)}})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{(bw_{A^{(l)}})}</annotation></semantics></math> entries), but also on accuracy: reducing <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{A^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{A^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> below 5 bits causes significant degradation for most models. The MNIST models are the most tolerant, maintaining near-baseline accuracy even at <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{A^{(l)}}\!=\!4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{A^{(l)}}\!=\!4</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{B^{(l)}}\!=\!3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{B^{(l)}}\!=\!3</annotation></semantics></math>, while the convolutional models degrade faster at low <math id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{A^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{A^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> values.</p>
</div>

<section id="S4.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.6" class="ltx_text">IV-B</span>2 </span>Accuracy vs Computational Complexity</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As mentioned, B-spline tabulation also further reduces computational complexity and runtime.
Concerning computational complexity, in Figure <a href="#S4.F11" title="Fig. 11 ‣ IV-B2 Accuracy vs Computational Complexity ‣ IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>, we report the Pareto front of accuracy versus BitOPs when combining B-spline tabulation with quantization. Compared to Figure <a href="#S4.F9" title="Fig. 9 ‣ IV-A Quantization Space Exploration: Accuracy vs BitOps ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>, the elimination of the Cox-de Boor evaluation shifts the Pareto front to significantly lower BitOPs, as the only remaining computational cost is the weight matrix multiplication. For instance, in Figure <a href="#S4.F9" title="Fig. 9 ‣ IV-A Quantization Space Exploration: Accuracy vs BitOps ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>(l) for ResKAN18, it was possible to reduce BitOPs by one order of magnitude (from <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 7\times 10^{8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>8</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 7\times 10^{8}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 7\times 10^{7}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>7</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 7\times 10^{7}</annotation></semantics></math>) without accuracy loss.
Considering both quantization and tabulation, the total BitOPs reduction from the FP32 baseline is substantial. For ResKAN18, from <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 4\times 10^{9}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>9</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 4\times 10^{9}</annotation></semantics></math> in Figure <a href="#S4.F9" title="Fig. 9 ‣ IV-A Quantization Space Exploration: Accuracy vs BitOps ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>(i) to <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 7\times 10^{7}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>7</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 7\times 10^{7}</annotation></semantics></math> in Figure <a href="#S4.F11" title="Fig. 11 ‣ IV-B2 Accuracy vs Computational Complexity ‣ IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>(l), i.e., more than <math id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="50\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\times</annotation></semantics></math> reduction without accuracy loss.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F11" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F11.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 11</span>: </span><span id="S4.F11.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Accuracy vs BitOPs trade-off for B-spline tabulation combined with quantization.
By replacing Cox-de Boor evaluation with a LUT, the B-spline computational cost is eliminated, leaving only the matrix multiplication.
The bit-width of <math id="S4.F11.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> is encoded by marker color, that of <math id="S4.F11.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> (LUT addressing) by marker size, and that of <math id="S4.F11.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> (LUT stored values) by marker shape.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS3.6" class="ltx_text">IV-B</span>3 </span>Latency Improvement</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="TABLE III ‣ IV-B3 Latency Improvement ‣ IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III</span></a>, we report the inference speedup on GPU obtained thanks to B-spline tabulation compared with the direct evaluation using the recursive Cox-de Boor formula (Eq. <a href="#S2.E2" title="In II-A Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks ‣ II Background and Motivation ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
As shown in the table, B-spline tabulation consistently accelerates inference across different grid size <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> values and model architectures, from single- and two-layer KAN MLPs for MNIST classification, to ConvKAN models based on LeNet and deeper CNNs,
and even ResNet-based ConvKAN. Tabulation yields <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.11" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.11</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.11</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.87\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.87</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.87\times</annotation></semantics></math> total speedup for <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G\!=\!3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo lspace="0.108em">=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G\!=\!3</annotation></semantics></math> and up to <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3.36\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.36</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.36\times</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G\!=\!5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo lspace="0.108em">=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G\!=\!5</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, GPUs only support specific bit-widths natively (e.g., 8-bit integer) and do not benefit from further reducing the B-spline table precision below 8 bits.
Custom hardware accelerators such as KAN-SAs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> can leverage lower-bit B-spline tables. Reducing the precision of the stored values shrinks each processing element (PE), allowing a larger systolic array to fit within the same area budget.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">

<tr id="S4.T3.6.16" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T3.6.16.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b"><math id="S4.T3.m59" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn mathsize="0.900em">5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="S4.T3.6.16.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_b"><math id="S4.T3.m60" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7969.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn mathsize="0.900em">7969.4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7969.4</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="S4.T3.6.16.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_b"><math id="S4.T3.m61" class="ltx_Math" alttext="84" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn mathsize="0.900em">84</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">84</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To quantify this effect on custom hardware, we synthesize a TPUv1-like <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite> accelerator using a KAN-SAs-style weight-stationary systolic array <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> as its compute core on an SQRL Acorn CLE-215+ board featuring a Xilinx Artix-7 xc7a200t FPGA.
All configurations use 8-bit weights and activations, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G\!=\!5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo lspace="0.108em">=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G\!=\!5</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P\!=\!3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0.108em">=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P\!=\!3</annotation></semantics></math>, and 256-entry B-spline lookup tables; only the B-spline table value bit-width varies.
In the KAN-SAs architecture, each PE stores a local copy of the B-spline lookup table. Thus, reducing the bit-width of the stored values shrinks each PE, freeing FPGA slices for additional PEs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T4" class="ltx_table">

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For each B-spline bit-width, the largest square systolic array that still fits within the FPGA’s slice budget is selected (i.e., increasing the array dimensions by one beyond those reported causes the design to exceed the available slices and fail place-and-route).
Note that in this TPUv1-like configuration, weight preload and matrix computation execute sequentially: the systolic array must be fully loaded with the current weight tile before input data can be streamed through. For single-sample inference, this per-tile preload overhead grows with the array dimensions and can offset the benefit of having more PEs, particularly when the layer dimensions are small relative to the array.
However, for batched inferences, the preload cost is amortized across all samples in the batch, making larger arrays strictly beneficial.
For each bit-width (B), Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="TABLE IV ‣ IV-B3 Latency Improvement ‣ IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV</span></a> reports the largest array dimension achieved, the FPGA resource utilization (Slice LUTs and Slices), the compute cycles (CC), and average measured inference time over 5 MNIST-shaped MLP workloads <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[784,n,10]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>784</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[784,n,10]</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\in\{32,64,128,192,256\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>32</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>64</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>128</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>192</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\in\{32,64,128,192,256\}</annotation></semantics></math> on the full test set (10 000 samples).
As shown, reducing the B-spline precision from 8 to 7 bits allows scaling the systolic array from <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="15\times 15" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>15</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15\times 15</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\times 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times 16</annotation></semantics></math>, yielding a measured <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.17\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.17</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.17\times</annotation></semantics></math> average speedup.
Reducing the precision further to 3 bits enables a <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20\times 20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\times 20</annotation></semantics></math> array, achieving a measured <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p4.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.24\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.24</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.24\times</annotation></semantics></math> average speedup over the 8-bit baseline.
The gap between estimated and measured speedup for larger arrays is due to DMA transfer overhead, which grows with the array dimensions due to memory bus alignment constraints.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">TABLE V</span>: </span><span id="S4.T5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Maximum clock frequency for a <math id="S4.T5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\times 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times 16</annotation></semantics></math> KAN-SAs systolic array with varying B-spline table bit-width on FPGA (<math id="S4.T5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W\!=\!8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0.128em">=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W\!=\!8</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.T5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G\!=\!5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo lspace="0.128em">=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G\!=\!5</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.T5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P\!=\!3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0.128em">=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P\!=\!3</annotation></semantics></math>).</span></figcaption>
<table id="S4.T5.5" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T5.5.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T5.5.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;">B</td>
<td id="S4.T5.5.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;" colspan="2">Slice LUTs</td>
<td id="S4.T5.5.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;">Max Freq</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T5.5.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T5.5.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;">(bits)</td>

</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond throughput, the area savings from B-spline quantization also enable higher clock frequencies.
To isolate this effect, Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="TABLE V ‣ IV-B3 Latency Improvement ‣ IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V</span></a> reports the maximum clock frequency achievable for a fixed <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\times 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times 16</annotation></semantics></math> array with each B-spline bit-width.
The 8-bit configuration cannot complete place-and-route for a <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\times 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times 16</annotation></semantics></math> array.
Reducing the bit-width to 7 bits allows the design to fit, but routing congestion at 93% LUT utilization limits the clock to 50 MHz.
Further quantization progressively reduces utilization and relieves routing pressure, enabling higher clock frequencies: 60 MHz at 6 bits, 70 MHz at 5 bits, and 75 MHz at 3 and 4 bits, a 50% improvement over the 7-bit baseline.
Alternatively, the freed resources could be used for architectural enhancements such as double-buffered weight preload to overlap tiling overhead with computation, or deeper on-chip buffers to hide memory latency.</p>
</div>

</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F12.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 12</span>: </span><span id="S4.F12.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Accuracy vs Spline Table Memory trade-off for spline tabulation.
The graphs show the Pareto front of accuracy versus total spline table memory cost for different bit-widths of <math id="S4.F12.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math> (marker size) and stored value precision <math id="S4.F12.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> (marker shape).</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To validate this, we run the 3-bit <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\times 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times 16</annotation></semantics></math> array at 75 MHz and measure the inference time for the KAN MLP <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[784,64,10]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>784</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>64</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[784,64,10]</annotation></semantics></math> on the full MNIST test set.
Compared to the 7-bit <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\times 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times 16</annotation></semantics></math> baseline at 50 MHz, the measured time drops from <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="185" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>185</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">185</annotation></semantics></math> ms to <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="129.55" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>129.55</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">129.55</annotation></semantics></math> ms, achieving a <math id="S4.SS2.SSS3.p6.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.43\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.43</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.43\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup.
Note that the achievable frequency remains limited by the high fanout of the control
signals across the systolic array, as the KAN-SAs design targets ASIC and is not optimized for FPGA.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS4.6" class="ltx_text">IV-B</span>4 </span>KAN-SAs Area and Frequency Scaling</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the impact of B-spline quantization on hardware independently of system-level effects, we synthesize the KAN-SAs <math id="S4.SS2.SSS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\times 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times 16</annotation></semantics></math> systolic array in isolation using Synopsys Design Compiler targeting ST 28nm FD-SOI technology.
Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="TABLE VI ‣ IV-B4 KAN-SAs Area and Frequency Scaling ‣ IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VI</span></a> reports the cell area and maximum achievable clock frequency for each configuration.
Halving both the B-spline and weight precision from 16 to 8 bits reduces the cell area by 60% (from 1 426k to 574k <math id="S4.SS2.SSS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu m^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu m^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> at 1 GHz) and raises the maximum frequency from 833 to 1 111 MHz.
Further reducing only the B-spline precision from 8 to 3 bits yields an additional 30% area reduction (to 403k <math id="S4.SS2.SSS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu m^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu m^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>) and increases the maximum frequency to 1 250 MHz, a 50% advantage over the 16-bit baseline.
Overall, the combined reduction from <math id="S4.SS2.SSS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B\!=\!16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0.108em">=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B\!=\!16</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W\!=\!16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0.108em">=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W\!=\!16</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS2.SSS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B\!=\!3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0.108em">=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B\!=\!3</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W\!=\!8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo lspace="0.108em">=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W\!=\!8</annotation></semantics></math> achieves a 72% area saving.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T6" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">TABLE VI</span>: </span><span id="S4.T6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">ASIC synthesis results for a <math id="S4.T6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\times 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times 16</annotation></semantics></math> KAN-SAs systolic array with varying B-spline and weight precision (ST 28nm FD-SOI, <math id="S4.T6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G\!=\!5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo lspace="0.128em">=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G\!=\!5</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.T6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P\!=\!3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0.128em">=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P\!=\!3</annotation></semantics></math>).</span></figcaption>

<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">IV-C</span> </span><span id="S4.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Spline Tabulation space exploration</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this subsection, we explore the space of possible quantized <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Spline</span> tabulation opportunities and show the effects in terms of accuracy vs. memory trade-off (Sec. <a href="#S4.SS3.SSS1" title="IV-C1 Accuracy vs Memory tradeoff of Spline Tabulation ‣ IV-C Spline Tabulation space exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-C1</span></a>) and inference latency (Sec. <a href="#S4.SS3.SSS2" title="IV-C2 Latency Improvement ‣ IV-C Spline Tabulation space exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-C2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.6" class="ltx_text">IV-C</span>1 </span>Accuracy vs Memory tradeoff of Spline Tabulation</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F12" title="Fig. 12 ‣ IV-B3 Latency Improvement ‣ IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> shows the Pareto front of accuracy versus total spline table memory for all models. The vertical dashed line indicates the total FP32 coefficient memory <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{l}N_{in}^{(l)}\cdot N_{out}^{(l)}\cdot(G+P)\cdot 32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>l</mi></msub><mrow><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{l}N_{in}^{(l)}\cdot N_{out}^{(l)}\cdot(G+P)\cdot 32</annotation></semantics></math> bits.
Tabulating a whole KAN leads to <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{l}N_{in}^{(l)}\cdot N_{out}^{(l)}\cdot 2^{(bw_{A^{(l)}})}\cdot h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>l</mi></msub><mrow><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{l}N_{in}^{(l)}\cdot N_{out}^{(l)}\cdot 2^{(bw_{A^{(l)}})}\cdot h</annotation></semantics></math> stored bits when using <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>-bit quantized spline values and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{(bw_{A^{(l)}})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{(bw_{A^{(l)}})}</annotation></semantics></math> table entries, as already mentioned in Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="III-C Spline Tabulation and Quantization ‣ III KANtize Approach ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III-C</span></a> for one layer.
For the MNIST models (KANMLP1, KANMLP2, LeKAN), several Pareto-optimal configurations lie to the left of this line with less than 1% accuracy drop, meaning the spline tables require less storage than the coefficients they replace. Specifically, <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{A^{(l)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{A^{(l)}}</annotation></semantics></math> can be reduced to as few as 4 bits and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> to 6 bits with negligible accuracy loss, consistent with prior studies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>.
For CIFAR-10, the sensitivity is model-dependent. CNN3, the smallest CIFAR-10 model, requires <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="bw_{A^{(l)}}\geq 7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><msup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></msub></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">bw_{A^{(l)}}\geq 7</annotation></semantics></math> bits to stay within <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}1\%</annotation></semantics></math> of full precision, while the deeper ResKAN18 is more sensitive to <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>, needing <math id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h\geq 7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h\geq 7</annotation></semantics></math> bits. Overall, under per-tensor post-training quantization alone, the table memory required to maintain accuracy exceeds the original coefficient storage by a wide margin, making spline tabulation impractical for larger models without additional compression.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.6" class="ltx_text">IV-C</span>2 </span>Latency Improvement</h4>
