</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T7" title="TABLE VII ‣ IV-C2 Latency Improvement ‣ IV-C Spline Tabulation space exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VII</span></a> reports the inference latency of spline tabulation compared to the baseline recursive B-spline-based execution.
As discussed in Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="III-C Spline Tabulation and Quantization ‣ III KANtize Approach ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III-C</span></a>, spline tabulation replaces the entire KAN layer with <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{in}\cdot N_{out}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{in}\cdot N_{out}</annotation></semantics></math> table lookups from the precomputed spline tables, followed by a summation along <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{in}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{in}</annotation></semantics></math> to produce each output, eliminating both the Cox-de Boor recursion and the coefficient matrix multiply.
Since each lookup contributes a single addition, the operation is inherently memory-bound, unlike the matrix multiply, which benefits from highly optimized GEMM implementations.
Thus, spline tabulation yields a net speedup only if the time saved by avoiding B-spline evaluation exceeds the cost of using memory-bound lookups instead of efficient matrix multiplication.
For small models (KANMLP1, KANMLP2, LeKAN), <span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">spline</span> tabulation yields speedups of <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.4</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="9.1\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>9.1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9.1\times</annotation></semantics></math> on GPU, as shown in Table <a href="#S4.T7" title="TABLE VII ‣ IV-C2 Latency Improvement ‣ IV-C Spline Tabulation space exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VII</span></a>. Indeed, the <span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">spline</span> tables remain reasonably small (see Figure <a href="#S4.F12" title="Fig. 12 ‣ IV-B3 Latency Improvement ‣ IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>), and, in the baseline version, the B-spline dominates the whole computation (see Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="TABLE III ‣ IV-B3 Latency Improvement ‣ IV-B B-Spline Tabulation Space Exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III</span></a>, BSP% column).
However, for larger models (CNN3, CNN4), the speedup drops significantly (down to <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="0.5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5\times</annotation></semantics></math> for CNN3 and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="0.1\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.1\times</annotation></semantics></math> for CNN4), while ResKAN18 achieves a <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.4\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.4\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup.
By analyzing this phenomenon, we observe that speedups depend on model depth and width: the baseline’s B-spline recursive evaluation is sequential and scales poorly with depth (requiring multiple kernel runs per layer). Conversely, increasing the layer width has little impact on its computation time, since GPUs can efficiently parallelize the element-wise operations across the width of each layer.
Concerning the ConvKAN layer’s spline tables, their indexing performs <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K^{2}\cdot C_{\text{in}}\cdot C_{\text{out}}\cdot H_{\text{out}}\cdot W_{\text{out}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K^{2}\cdot C_{\text{in}}\cdot C_{\text{out}}\cdot H_{\text{out}}\cdot W_{\text{out}}</annotation></semantics></math> scattered memory reads. A deep model distributes reads across many independent kernel runs while maintaining good memory locality, whereas increasing layer width degrades memory throughput by concentrating lookups into a single kernel.
Therefore, ResKAN18 requires more B-spline time due to its deeper architecture (<math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>20</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20</annotation></semantics></math> layers), despite narrower layers, as confirmed in Figure <a href="#S4.F13" title="Fig. 13 ‣ IV-C2 Latency Improvement ‣ IV-C Spline Tabulation space exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>. CNN4’s final layer (resolution <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8\times 8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8\times 8</annotation></semantics></math>) requires <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>64</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64</annotation></semantics></math> accesses per table per sample, whereas ResKAN18’s smaller layers (<math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\times 2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times 2</annotation></semantics></math>) require only <math id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math> accesses.
In summary, <span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">spline tabulation</span> is slower than the baseline recursive B-spline for CNN3 and CNN4 because the cumulative lookup cost exceeds the savings from reduced recursion.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F13" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2603.17230v1/kernel_gantt.svg" id="S4.F13.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:429/350;" width="429" height="350"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F13.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 13</span>: </span><span id="S4.F13.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">CUDA kernel time breakdown for baseline (Cox-de Boor) vs spline tabulation on CNN3, CNN4, and ResKAN18
(<math id="S4.F13.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G\!=\!3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo lspace="0.128em">=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G\!=\!3</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.F13.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P\!=\!3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0.128em">=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P\!=\!3</annotation></semantics></math>, RTX3090).</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS3.6" class="ltx_text">IV-C</span>3 </span>Scalability of Spline Tabulation on FPGA</h4>

<figure id="S4.F14" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2603.17230v1/params_vs_luts.svg" id="S4.F14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/339;" width="452" height="339"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F14.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 14</span>: </span><span id="S4.F14.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Estimated FPGA LUT cost of spline tabulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> for the models studied in this paper. The dashed red line indicates the capacity of a Virtex UltraScale+ FPGA. Horizontal green lines report KAN-SAs systolic array <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> configurations, labeled by B-spline coefficient precision <math id="S4.F14.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>, weight precision <math id="S4.F14.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math>, activation precision <math id="S4.F14.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>, and array dimensions.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{in}\cdot N_{out}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{in}\cdot N_{out}</annotation></semantics></math> scaling of spline tabulation, which limits GPU speedups for larger models (as shown in Table <a href="#S4.T7" title="TABLE VII ‣ IV-C2 Latency Improvement ‣ IV-C Spline Tabulation space exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VII</span></a>), also poses a challenge for FPGA implementations. In an approach such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, each spline connection requires independent FPGA LUTs, leading to a total resource cost proportional to <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{l}N_{in}^{(l)}\cdot N_{out}^{(l)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>l</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{l}N_{in}^{(l)}\cdot N_{out}^{(l)}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> explored spline tabulation implementations on various FPGAs, including mid-range and high-end devices such as Zynq UltraScale+ and Virtex UltraScale+.
Figure <a href="#S4.F14" title="Fig. 14 ‣ IV-C3 Scalability of Spline Tabulation on FPGA ‣ IV-C Spline Tabulation space exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> shows the estimated FPGA LUT cost for the models studied in this paper, using an empirical cost of approximately <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9</annotation></semantics></math> FPGA LUTs per connection derived from the synthesis results reported in the ablation study in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> for 6-bit addressed, 8-bit valued spline tables on a Xilinx Virtex UltraScale+, a high-end FPGA family.
The graph shows that the spline tabulation approach remains viable for models of limited dimensions, such as KANMLP1, KANMLP2, LeKAN, and CNN3. However, it does not scale well for larger models, such as CNN4 and ResKAN18, exceeding the available resources by orders of magnitude on a high-end FPGA.
Using aggressive pruning (<math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}98\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mn>98</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}98\%</annotation></semantics></math>) combined with quantization-aware training via Brevitas <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>, the work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> manages to reduce the cost of a KANMLP2 variant to <math id="S4.SS3.SSS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3809" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3809</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3809</annotation></semantics></math> LUTs on a Zynq UltraScale+, albeit with 1-bit input addressing and only after pruning and re-training.
Whether such extreme pruning is feasible on more complex tasks and datasets remains to be determined, thus leaving open questions about the scalability of the spline tabulation approach.
In contrast, the KAN-SAs-like systolic array <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> accelerators have a constant area footprint regardless of model size, as shown by the horizontal lines in Figure <a href="#S4.F14" title="Fig. 14 ‣ IV-C3 Scalability of Spline Tabulation on FPGA ‣ IV-C Spline Tabulation space exploration ‣ IV Experimental Results ‣ KANtize: Exploring Low-bit Quantization of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Efficient Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">V </span><span id="S5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Conclusion</span></h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) have attracted much attention for their promise of better parameter efficiency and interpretability than Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs). Nevertheless, their reliance on evaluating spline functions, often expressed as linear combinations of weighted basis splines (B-splines), poses a significant computational challenge.
In this paper, we investigated the impact of low-bit quantization on KANs’ accuracy as well as its benefits in reducing computational complexity and improving hardware efficiency. Our experiments revealed that B-splines are highly robust to quantization, i.e., down to 2-3 bits without loss of accuracy, and yield substantial reductions in computational complexity, whereas the learnable weights are more sensitive to quantization.
Moreover, the computational overhead introduced by B-splines recursive evaluation, can be reduced through B-spline tabulation. Hence, we evaluate the impact of quantization on tabulation and their joint benefits for computational complexity and hardware efficiency.
Our experiments showed that a BitOps reduction of more than <math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="50\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\times</annotation></semantics></math> is possible, e.g., for ResKAN18, without accuracy loss thanks to quantized B-spline tabulation. Moreover, we obtained up to <math id="S5.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.9\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.9</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.9\times</annotation></semantics></math> inference speedup on GPUs thanks to B-spline tabulation, and up to 36% resource reduction, 50% higher clock frequency and <math id="S5.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.24\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.24</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.24\times</annotation></semantics></math> inference speedup on FPGA thanks to quantized B-spline tabulation. On 28nm FD-SOI ASIC, a 72% area reduction and 50% higher maximum frequency was obtained. Finally, we explored the opportunities and limitations of a similar state-of-the-art approach tabulating the entire <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">splines</span> instead of the B-splines, highlighting its convenience compared to the B-spline tabulation for models of limited dimension, whereas its scalability becomes challenging for larger models.</p>
</div>
</section>
